lesson.title: The Circuit's Engine: Ideal and Real Voltage Sources
lesson.summary: Explains the ideal voltage source model and its schematic symbol, then shows how real batteries deviate from that ideal because of internal resistance, using a worked terminal voltage example.
lesson.body:
You already know voltage as a potential difference, and you can now recognize the schematic symbol for a battery as two unequal parallel lines. A voltage source is the circuit element built specifically to establish and maintain a chosen potential difference between two terminals, supplying whatever current the rest of the circuit demands to keep that voltage fixed. In schematics, an ideal voltage source is often drawn as a circle with plus and minus signs marking its terminals, distinguishing it from the simpler battery symbol used for real, physical cells.

The word ideal is doing real work in that description. An ideal voltage source holds its terminal voltage exactly constant no matter how much current is drawn from it, from a single microamp to thousands of amps, which is a convenient fiction for analysis but not something any physical device achieves. Real sources, including batteries, generators, and power supplies, all have some internal resistance that causes their terminal voltage to sag as current draw increases. This internal resistance is usually modeled as a small resistor in series with an ideal voltage source inside the device.

Consider a 9 volt battery with an internal resistance of 0.5 ohms, connected to a circuit that draws 100 milliamps, or 0.1 amps. The internal resistance causes an internal voltage drop of I times r, equal to 0.1 A times 0.5 ohms, or 0.05 volts. The terminal voltage actually available to the external circuit is therefore 9 minus 0.05, or 8.95 volts, slightly less than the battery's rated 9 volts. Draw more current, say 2 amps during a heavy load, and the drop grows to 1 volt, leaving only 8 volts at the terminals, which is why batteries feel weaker under heavy load and recover somewhat once the load is removed.

This behavior explains several everyday observations. A flashlight dims noticeably right when a motor or heating element switches on elsewhere in the same battery powered device, because the sudden current draw increases the internal voltage drop and briefly pulls down the terminal voltage available to everything else on that battery. It is also why device datasheets and battery specifications often list an internal resistance or an equivalent series resistance value, since that number predicts how much the voltage will sag under a specified current.

For most introductory circuit analysis, though, treating a source as ideal, with zero internal resistance, is a reasonable simplification as long as the current drawn stays well below whatever level would make the internal drop significant. As your circuits get more advanced, keeping the real, non ideal behavior of sources in mind becomes essential, particularly when precision matters or when a circuit draws current close to a source's rated maximum.

One more useful idea follows directly from this internal resistance model: a real source can only deliver its maximum possible power to a load under a specific condition, when the load resistance equals the source's own internal resistance, a result known as the maximum power transfer principle. Mismatched loads, either much larger or much smaller than the internal resistance, still work fine electrically but waste a larger fraction of the available power inside the source itself rather than delivering it usefully to the load, which is a design consideration that shows up repeatedly in audio equipment and radio frequency systems.
